questions.question: What is the largest fish in the sea?
questions.explanation: The whale shark is the biggest fish alive. Despite its size, it is a gentle filter feeder that eats plankton and small fish.

questions.question: What is the largest animal alive today?
questions.explanation: The blue whale is the largest animal alive today, reaching nearly 100 feet long.

questions.question: What tiny shrimp-like animals are the main food of blue whales?
questions.explanation: Blue whales feed almost entirely on krill, gulping huge mouthfuls and straining the water out through their baleen.

questions.question: How do dolphins find prey in dark or murky water?
questions.explanation: Dolphins send out clicks and listen for the echoes. This echolocation lets them map their surroundings and find fish by sound.

questions.question: Which sea turtle is named for the tough, rubbery skin it has in place of a hard shell?
questions.explanation: The leatherback has no hard bony shell. Its back is covered in thick, leathery skin over a layer of oily tissue.

questions.question: How many arms does an octopus have?
questions.explanation: An octopus has eight arms lined with suckers. Squid and cuttlefish have eight arms plus two longer feeding tentacles.

questions.question: How many hearts does an octopus have?
questions.explanation: An octopus has three hearts: two pump blood through the gills, and one pumps it around the rest of the body.

questions.question: What do octopus and squid squirt into the water to escape predators?
questions.explanation: Octopus and squid release a cloud of dark ink that confuses predators while they jet away.

questions.question: What tiny animals build coral reefs?
questions.explanation: Reefs are built by coral polyps, small soft animals that lay down hard limestone skeletons over thousands of years.

questions.question: The Great Barrier Reef lies off the coast of which country?
questions.explanation: The Great Barrier Reef stretches along the northeast coast of Australia and is the largest coral reef system on Earth.

questions.question: Which of these body parts does a jellyfish lack?
questions.explanation: Jellyfish have no brain. A simple net of nerves lets them sense touch, light and movement and react.

questions.question: What do hermit crabs use as a home to protect their soft bodies?
questions.explanation: Hermit crabs tuck their soft bellies into empty snail shells and move into bigger ones as they grow.

questions.question: The orca, or killer whale, is the largest member of which family?
questions.explanation: Despite the name killer whale, the orca is the largest member of the dolphin family.

questions.question: What is a baby whale called?
questions.explanation: A baby whale is a calf. It nurses on its mother's rich milk and stays close to her for months or years.

questions.question: What is the breathing opening on top of a whale's head called?
questions.explanation: Whales breathe through a blowhole on top of the head, so they can grab air without lifting their whole head out of the water.

questions.question: A narwhal's long spiral tusk is actually what?
questions.explanation: The narwhal's tusk is a long tooth that grows out through its upper lip, mostly in males.

questions.question: Which seabird with a bright, striped beak is nicknamed the sea parrot?
questions.explanation: Atlantic puffins grow colorful beaks in breeding season, which earned them the nickname sea parrot.

questions.question: Which bird has the widest wingspan of any living bird?
questions.explanation: The wandering albatross has the widest wingspan of any living bird, reaching about 11 feet tip to tip.

questions.question: What do giant manta rays mainly eat?
questions.explanation: Manta rays are filter feeders. They swim with their mouths open, sieving tiny plankton from the water.

questions.question: Where is a stingray's venomous spine?
questions.explanation: A stingray's barbed spine sits on its tail. It uses it only in defense, usually when stepped on.

questions.question: Which animal uses its long tusks to haul itself out onto the ice?
questions.explanation: Walruses hook their tusks into the ice to drag their heavy bodies up. Their genus name, Odobenus, means tooth walker.

questions.question: What do sea otters use as tools to crack open shellfish?
questions.explanation: Sea otters float on their backs and smash clams and urchins against a rock held on their chest.

questions.question: Where do female sea turtles lay their eggs?
questions.explanation: Female sea turtles crawl ashore at night, dig a nest in the sand, lay their eggs and return to the sea.

questions.question: What color does a lobster shell usually turn when it is cooked?
questions.explanation: Heat breaks apart the proteins that hold a red pigment called astaxanthin, letting the bright red show through.

questions.question: Which way do most crabs walk?
questions.explanation: Most crabs walk sideways because their leg joints bend outward, which makes a sideways scuttle their fastest gait.

questions.question: Wild penguins live almost entirely in which part of the world?
questions.explanation: Penguins live almost entirely south of the equator, from Antarctica to the coasts of Africa, South America and Australia.

questions.question: Which whale is famous for singing long, complex songs?
questions.explanation: Male humpback whales sing long, repeating songs that can last for hours. Whales in the same region share and slowly change the tune.

questions.question: What is the largest whale with teeth?
questions.explanation: The sperm whale is the largest toothed whale. Bigger giants like the blue whale use baleen instead of teeth.

questions.question: Which white Arctic whale is nicknamed the sea canary?
questions.explanation: Belugas chirp, whistle and click so much that sailors called them sea canaries.

questions.question: What happens when a shark loses a tooth?
questions.explanation: Sharks have rows of spare teeth behind the front ones. When a tooth falls out, a new one rolls forward to replace it.

questions.question: What does a pelican use its big throat pouch for?
questions.explanation: A pelican's stretchy pouch scoops up fish and water together. It drains the water out, then swallows the fish.

questions.question: Water that stays too warm for too long often makes coral do what?
questions.explanation: Heat stress makes corals expel the algae living in their tissue, leaving them white. Long bleaching can starve and kill a reef.

questions.question: Which jellyfish, shaped like a cube, carries some of the most dangerous venom in the sea?
questions.explanation: Box jellyfish are named for their cube-shaped bell. Some species carry venom strong enough to be deadly to swimmers.

questions.question: Male elephant seals are named for what feature?
questions.explanation: Adult male elephant seals grow a large, drooping nose like a short trunk, which helps them roar during fights.

questions.question: Which Antarctic seal is a top hunter of penguins?
questions.explanation: Leopard seals are spotted, powerful predators that often wait near the ice edge to catch penguins in the water.

questions.question: Manatees are often called by what nickname?
questions.explanation: Manatees are called sea cows because they slowly graze on seagrass and water plants, like cattle in a field.

questions.question: What is a group of dolphins or whales usually called?
questions.explanation: Whales and dolphins travel in groups called pods, often made up of family members who hunt and travel together.

questions.question: The tiger shark is named for what?
questions.explanation: Young tiger sharks have dark stripes down their sides, like a tiger. The stripes fade as the shark grows.

questions.question: Which sea turtle is named for its big, blocky head?
questions.explanation: Loggerheads have large heads and powerful jaws that let them crush hard-shelled prey like crabs and conchs.

questions.question: How does a crab grow bigger?
questions.explanation: A crab's shell cannot grow, so it molts. It crawls out of the old shell and swells up before the new soft shell hardens.

questions.question: What color is octopus blood?
questions.explanation: Octopus blood uses a copper-based protein called hemocyanin to carry oxygen, which turns it blue.

questions.question: What decides whether a sea turtle hatchling is male or female?
questions.explanation: Sea turtle sex is set by the warmth of the sand. Warmer nests produce mostly females, cooler nests mostly males.

questions.question: How do dolphins sleep without drowning?
options: Half a brain at a time
questions.explanation: Dolphins rest one half of the brain at a time. The awake half keeps them surfacing to breathe and watching for danger.

questions.question: The Portuguese man o' war was named after what?
questions.explanation: Its floating, sail-like gas bladder reminded sailors of an old armed sailing ship, the man-of-war.

questions.question: What do sea lions have that true seals lack?
questions.explanation: Sea lions have small outer ear flaps. True seals have only ear holes, which makes their heads look smooth.

questions.question: The dugong's closest living relatives on land are which animals?
questions.explanation: Dugongs and manatees share a common ancestor with elephants, despite living their whole lives in the water.

questions.question: Which shark is famous for swimming far up freshwater rivers?
questions.explanation: Bull sharks can handle fresh water and have been found far up rivers such as the Mississippi and the Amazon.

questions.question: How does a thresher shark stun its prey?
questions.explanation: Thresher sharks have a tail fin nearly as long as their body. They whip it through schools of fish to stun them.

questions.question: Which shark is widely considered the fastest swimmer?
questions.explanation: The shortfin mako is built like a torpedo and can put on bursts of great speed, even leaping clear of the water.

questions.question: Which ray can stun its prey with an electric shock?
questions.explanation: Torpedo rays have organs in their wide fins that release electric shocks to stun prey and fend off attackers.

questions.question: What is the nickname for a shark or skate egg case washed up on the beach?
questions.explanation: Shark and skate egg cases are tough pouches often found on beaches, long known as mermaid's purses.

questions.question: Gray whales give birth in warm lagoons off which country?
questions.explanation: Eastern Pacific gray whales migrate from Arctic feeding grounds to calve in the lagoons of Baja California, Mexico.

questions.question: What do humpback whales blow to trap schools of fish?
questions.explanation: Humpbacks swim in a spiral while blowing bubbles, forming a net that traps fish before the whales lunge up through it.

questions.question: Bottlenose dolphins use unique signature whistles that work much like what?
questions.explanation: Each bottlenose dolphin develops its own signature whistle, and others copy it to call that dolphin, much like a name.

questions.question: What land animal is the closest living relative of whales and dolphins?
questions.explanation: Whales and hippos share a common ancestor. Whales evolved from land mammals that took to the water around 50 million years ago.

questions.question: The so-called immortal jellyfish can escape death by doing what?
questions.explanation: When stressed or injured, Turritopsis dohrnii can turn back into its young polyp stage and start its life over.

questions.question: What do hawksbill turtles feed on most?
questions.explanation: Hawksbills use their narrow, pointed beaks to pick sponges from reef crevices. Few other animals can eat sponges.

questions.question: What do leatherback turtles mainly eat?
questions.explanation: Leatherbacks feed mostly on jellyfish. Backward-pointing spines in their throats help hold the slippery prey.

questions.question: Male frigatebirds inflate what to attract a mate?
questions.explanation: Male frigatebirds puff up a bright red throat pouch like a balloon to catch the eye of females flying overhead.

questions.question: What special skin cells let an octopus change color in an instant?
questions.explanation: Octopuses have thousands of chromatophores, tiny sacs of pigment that their muscles stretch or squeeze to change color.

questions.question: What is the only hard part of an octopus's body?
questions.explanation: An octopus has no bones. Its beak is its only hard part, so it can squeeze through any gap wider than its beak.

questions.question: The blue-ringed octopus carries the same deadly toxin as which fish?
questions.explanation: Blue-ringed octopuses carry tetrodotoxin, the same nerve toxin found in pufferfish, made by bacteria in their bodies.

questions.question: What is the largest known species of octopus?
questions.explanation: The giant Pacific octopus is the largest known octopus, with arms that can span several yards from tip to tip.

questions.question: What does a cuttlefish's cuttlebone help it control?
questions.explanation: The cuttlebone is a light, chambered inner shell. The cuttlefish moves gas and fluid in and out of it to rise or sink.

questions.question: Which shelled relative of the octopus has dozens of tentacles and a chambered shell?
questions.explanation: The nautilus lives in a coiled shell divided into chambers. It adjusts the gas in those chambers to float, and has up to about 90 tentacles.

questions.question: How do squid make a fast getaway?
questions.explanation: Squid fill their mantle with water and force it out through a funnel called a siphon, shooting off like a jet.

questions.question: Horseshoe crabs are more closely related to which animals than to true crabs?
questions.explanation: Despite the name, horseshoe crabs are not crabs. They are closer kin to spiders and scorpions.

questions.question: Which crab has the longest leg span of any arthropod?
questions.explanation: The Japanese spider crab can spread its legs about 12 feet from tip to tip, the widest of any arthropod.

questions.question: Which reef crustacean strikes prey with one of the fastest punches in nature?
questions.explanation: Mantis shrimp swing club-like limbs so fast they can crack snail shells and even aquarium glass.

questions.question: How do puffins carry several small fish home at once?
questions.explanation: Puffins grip fish crosswise in their beaks, using a spiny tongue to hold the catch while they snap up more.

questions.question: Millions of red crabs march to the sea each year on which island?
questions.explanation: Each year on Christmas Island, millions of red crabs leave the forest and migrate to the coast to release their eggs into the sea.

questions.question: Corals are most closely related to which animals?
questions.explanation: Corals belong to the same group as sea anemones and jellyfish, simple animals that catch food with stinging tentacles.

questions.question: Reef-building corals get most of their food from what living inside them?
questions.explanation: Reef corals host tiny algae in their tissue. The algae turn sunlight into food and share it, giving corals most of their energy.

questions.question: Which sea star is notorious for eating coral reefs?
questions.explanation: Crown-of-thorns sea stars feed on coral polyps. Big outbreaks of them can strip large patches of reef bare.

questions.question: Many reef corals spawn together on the same few nights, timed mainly by what?
questions.explanation: Mass coral spawning is cued by water temperature and timed to the night by the phase of the moon, releasing clouds of eggs at once.

questions.question: Sawfish, with their long toothy snouts, are actually a kind of what?
questions.explanation: Sawfish are rays with a long, toothed snout. Their gills sit on their undersides, unlike the look-alike sawsharks.

questions.question: What are the tiny tooth-like scales covering a shark's skin called?
questions.explanation: Shark skin is covered in dermal denticles, tiny tooth-like scales that cut drag and feel like sandpaper when rubbed backward.

questions.question: The wobbegong, with its fringed beard, is a type of what?
questions.explanation: Wobbegongs are carpet sharks that lie camouflaged on the reef floor, ambushing fish that wander too close.

questions.question: Which small shark bites round plugs of flesh out of much larger animals?
questions.explanation: The cookiecutter shark latches on with its lips and twists, leaving a neat round wound on whales, seals and big fish.

questions.question: What can scientists count in a whale's earwax plug to estimate its age?
questions.explanation: Baleen whales build up earwax plugs in layers over their lives. Counting the bands, like tree rings, gives the whale's age.

questions.question: What waxy substance, once prized for perfume, forms in a sperm whale's gut?
questions.explanation: Ambergris forms in the guts of some sperm whales. It was long valued in perfume for its sweet, earthy scent.

questions.question: Which whale may live over 200 years, among the longest of any mammal?
questions.explanation: Bowhead whales live in Arctic waters and can pass 200 years, based on chemical clues in their eyes and old harpoon tips.

questions.question: The vaquita, the world's smallest porpoise, lives only in which waters?
questions.explanation: The vaquita is found only in the northern Gulf of California, Mexico, one of the smallest ranges of any marine mammal.

questions.question: Which Antarctic seal keeps its breathing holes open by rasping the ice with its teeth?
questions.explanation: Weddell seals live under the Antarctic sea ice and saw at their breathing holes with their teeth to stop them freezing over.

questions.question: The group name pinniped, for seals, sea lions and walruses, means what?
questions.explanation: Pinniped comes from Latin words meaning fin or feather footed, a nod to their flippers.

questions.question: How did the green sea turtle get its name?
questions.explanation: Green turtles are named for the greenish color of their body fat, not their shell, which is brown or olive.

questions.question: What Spanish word names the mass nesting events of ridley sea turtles?
questions.explanation: In an arribada, meaning arrival, thousands of ridley turtles come ashore together over a few nights to lay eggs.

questions.question: Which squid is the heaviest known invertebrate?
questions.explanation: The colossal squid of the Southern Ocean is shorter than the giant squid but much heavier, the heaviest invertebrate known.

questions.question: The vampire squid's Latin name roughly translates to what?
questions.explanation: Its name, Vampyroteuthis infernalis, means vampire squid from hell, though it is small, gentle and eats drifting debris.

questions.question: Fishers nicknamed the Humboldt squid for its color flashes and fierce hunting. What is it called?
questions.explanation: Humboldt squid flash red and white as they hunt in groups, which earned them the nickname red devil.

questions.question: Where are most of an octopus's nerve cells found?
questions.explanation: About two thirds of an octopus's neurons are in its arms, which can taste, feel and react with little input from the brain.

questions.question: How does a snapping shrimp stun its prey?
questions.explanation: Snapping shrimp close a special claw so fast it shoots out a bubble. The bubble collapses with a loud crack that stuns small prey.

questions.question: Which naturalist first explained how coral atolls form around sinking islands?
questions.explanation: Darwin proposed that reefs keep growing upward as volcanic islands slowly sink, leaving a ring of coral around a lagoon.

questions.question: What are the stinging cells of jellyfish called?
questions.explanation: Jellyfish tentacles are packed with nematocysts, tiny capsules that fire a coiled, venom-tipped thread when touched.

questions.question: Besides a bloom, what is a group of jellyfish called?
questions.explanation: A group of jellyfish can be called a smack, as well as a bloom or a swarm.

questions.question: What do comb jellies use to swim?
questions.explanation: Comb jellies move by beating rows of tiny hairs called cilia. The rows scatter light into shimmering rainbows.

questions.question: What technique lets albatrosses cross oceans with barely a wingbeat?
questions.explanation: Dynamic soaring uses the change in wind speed just above the waves. Albatrosses swing up into the wind and back down, gaining energy each loop.

questions.question: Albatrosses and petrels belong to a group nicknamed for their nostrils. What is it?
questions.explanation: Tubenoses have nostrils in tubes on their beaks. They help sniff out food across the open sea and drain away excess salt.

questions.question: The humpback whale's scientific name, Megaptera, means what?
questions.explanation: Megaptera means big wing, after the humpback's huge flippers, the longest of any whale.

questions.question: What is it called when a dead whale sinks and feeds deep-sea life for years?
questions.explanation: A whale fall is a whale carcass on the deep seafloor. It can feed scavengers, worms and bacteria for decades.

questions.question: Which is the smallest of the world's five oceans?
questions.explanation: The Arctic Ocean is the smallest and shallowest of the five oceans, wrapped around the North Pole.

questions.question: What mostly causes the ocean's tides?
questions.explanation: The Moon's gravity pulls the oceans into bulges, and Earth turning beneath them makes the tides rise and fall.

questions.question: How many high tides do most coasts get in a day?
questions.explanation: Most coasts see two high tides and two low tides in roughly a day.

questions.question: Which strait joins the Mediterranean Sea to the Atlantic Ocean?
questions.explanation: The Strait of Gibraltar runs between Spain and Morocco and is the Mediterranean's door to the Atlantic.

questions.question: Which cape at the bottom of South America is feared for its storms?
questions.explanation: Cape Horn sits where the Atlantic meets the Pacific, and its gales and big seas wrecked many sailing ships.

questions.question: What is a huge ocean wave set off by an undersea earthquake called?
questions.explanation: A tsunami forms when an earthquake, landslide or eruption shoves a vast amount of seawater at once.

questions.question: What is a hurricane called in the western Pacific?
questions.explanation: The same kind of tropical storm is a hurricane in the Atlantic and a typhoon in the western Pacific.

questions.question: Which ocean circles all the way around Antarctica?
questions.explanation: The Southern Ocean surrounds Antarctica, with no land breaking its ring.

questions.question: Which canal lets ships cross Central America between two oceans?
questions.explanation: The Panama Canal links the Atlantic and Pacific, sparing ships the long trip around South America.

questions.question: Which canal links the Mediterranean Sea and the Red Sea?
questions.explanation: The Suez Canal cuts through Egypt, joining the Mediterranean to the Red Sea.

questions.question: Not counting Australia, what is the largest island on Earth?
questions.explanation: Greenland is the world's largest island. Australia is counted as a continent instead.

questions.question: A falling barometer aboard ship usually warns of what?
questions.explanation: A barometer measures air pressure. Falling pressure often means a storm or low pressure system is on its way.

questions.question: Where do hurricanes get most of their energy?
questions.explanation: Hurricanes feed on heat and moisture from warm sea surfaces, which is why they weaken over land.

questions.question: What is the calm center of a hurricane called?
questions.explanation: The eye is a calm, often clear patch at the storm's center, ringed by the fierce winds of the eyewall.

questions.question: Which sea lies between southern Europe and northern Africa?
questions.explanation: The Mediterranean is nearly enclosed by land, with Europe to the north and Africa to the south.

questions.question: Which is the second largest ocean on Earth?
questions.explanation: The Atlantic is second in size after the Pacific.

questions.question: What do sailors call the calm, windless band near the equator?
questions.explanation: Sailing ships could sit becalmed for days in the doldrums, a low pressure belt near the equator.

questions.question: The Cape of Good Hope lies at the southern end of which continent?
questions.explanation: The Cape of Good Hope is a rocky headland near Cape Town, South Africa.

questions.question: Which narrow strait separates Asia from North America?
questions.explanation: The Bering Strait lies between Russia and Alaska and joins the Pacific to the Arctic Ocean.

questions.question: What is the highest point of a wave called?
questions.explanation: The crest is the top of a wave. The low point between two waves is the trough.

questions.question: What is a strong, narrow current that pulls swimmers away from the beach?
questions.explanation: Rip currents carry water back out to sea through gaps in the surf. Swimmers escape by swimming parallel to shore.

questions.question: What is the falling tide, as water drains away from shore, called?
questions.explanation: The tide ebbs as it falls and floods as it rises.

questions.question: Roughly how much of an iceberg sits below the waterline?
questions.explanation: Ice is only a little lighter than seawater, so around 90 percent of an iceberg floats hidden underwater.

questions.question: In which ocean did the Titanic sink in 1912?
questions.explanation: The Titanic struck an iceberg and sank in the North Atlantic on its first voyage, bound for New York.

questions.question: Which sea lies between northeast Africa and the Arabian Peninsula?
questions.explanation: The Red Sea is a long, narrow arm of the Indian Ocean between Africa and Arabia.

questions.question: Off which country's coast lies the Great Barrier Reef?
questions.explanation: The Great Barrier Reef runs along Queensland in northeast Australia and is the largest coral reef system on Earth.

questions.question: Which scale do sailors use to rate the strength of the wind?
questions.explanation: The Beaufort scale runs from force 0, calm, up to force 12, hurricane, judged by how the sea looks.

questions.question: On a sunny day at the coast, which way does a sea breeze blow?
questions.explanation: Land heats faster than water by day, so warm air rises over land and cooler sea air flows in to replace it.

questions.question: What creates most of the waves on the open ocean?
questions.explanation: Wind blowing across the water drives most ocean waves. Stronger, longer winds make bigger waves.

questions.question: The Ring of Fire, a belt of volcanoes and earthquakes, rims which ocean?
questions.explanation: The Ring of Fire traces the edges of the Pacific, where tectonic plates meet and grind.

questions.question: What do you call a tornado that forms over water?
questions.explanation: A waterspout is a spinning column of air over water, often seen in warm seas.

questions.question: Finish the old sailors' rhyme: Red sky at night...
questions.explanation: A red evening sky often means clear, dry air to the west, where most weather comes from in the mid latitudes.

questions.question: The big island of Madagascar sits in which ocean?
questions.explanation: Madagascar lies in the Indian Ocean off the southeast coast of Africa.

questions.question: Which sea is bordered by the islands of the Greater and Lesser Antilles?
questions.explanation: The Antilles island chains form the northern and eastern edges of the Caribbean Sea.

questions.question: Which shallow sea lies between Great Britain and Scandinavia?
questions.explanation: The North Sea sits between Britain, Norway, Denmark, Germany and the Low Countries.

questions.question: What do ships use to measure depth by bouncing sound off the seafloor?
questions.explanation: Sonar sends a sound pulse down and times its echo. Sound's speed in water turns that time into depth.

questions.question: The Galapagos Islands belong to which country?
questions.explanation: The Galapagos lie in the Pacific about 1,000 km off Ecuador, which governs them.

questions.question: Which compound makes up most of the salt in seawater?
questions.explanation: Sodium and chloride ions make up most of the sea's dissolved salt, the same stuff as table salt.

questions.question: What is a ring-shaped coral reef around a lagoon called?
questions.explanation: An atoll is a ring of coral reef or islets enclosing a lagoon, common in the tropical Pacific and Indian oceans.

questions.question: What are the extra-large tides near a new or full moon called?
questions.explanation: When Sun and Moon line up at new and full moon, their pulls combine into spring tides. The name has nothing to do with the season.

questions.question: What are the weakest tides, near a quarter moon, called?
questions.explanation: At quarter moons the Sun and Moon pull at right angles, so the gap between high and low tide is smallest.

questions.question: The Gulf Stream is named for which gulf?
questions.explanation: The Gulf Stream flows out of the Gulf of Mexico region, past Florida and up the US East Coast.

questions.question: Which cold current flows north along the west coast of South America?
questions.explanation: The Humboldt, or Peru, Current brings cold, rich water up the coast and feeds huge fisheries.

questions.question: In the Northern Hemisphere, the Coriolis effect bends moving water which way?
questions.explanation: Earth's spin deflects moving air and water to the right in the north and to the left in the south.

questions.question: About how many grams of salt are in a kilogram of average seawater?
questions.explanation: Average ocean salinity is about 35 parts per thousand, or roughly 35 grams of salt per kilogram of water.

questions.question: The Bosporus strait links the Sea of Marmara with which sea?
questions.explanation: The Bosporus runs through Istanbul and is the Black Sea's only path toward the Mediterranean.

questions.question: The Strait of Hormuz is the only sea passage out of which gulf?
questions.explanation: The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea.

questions.question: Which Portuguese explorer first sailed around the Cape of Good Hope?
questions.explanation: Bartolomeu Dias rounded the cape in 1488, opening the sea route that da Gama later sailed to India.

questions.question: Which Canadian bay is famous for having the highest tides in the world?
questions.explanation: The Bay of Fundy's shape funnels the tide so it can rise and fall more than 15 meters.

questions.question: Each day, high tide arrives about how much later than the day before?
questions.explanation: A lunar day is about 24 hours 50 minutes, because the Moon moves along its orbit, so tides slip later each day.

questions.question: The warm Kuroshio Current flows past which country?
questions.explanation: The Kuroshio is the Pacific's answer to the Gulf Stream, carrying warm water north along Japan.

questions.question: Which cold current carries icebergs south past Newfoundland?
questions.explanation: The Labrador Current flows down from the Arctic along Canada, bringing icebergs into the North Atlantic shipping lanes.

questions.question: What is the height difference between high tide and low tide called?
questions.explanation: The tidal range is how far the water rises and falls. It is largest at spring tides.

questions.question: How long is one international nautical mile?
questions.explanation: A nautical mile is 1,852 meters, close to one minute of latitude. A knot is one nautical mile per hour.

questions.question: What do sailors call the strong westerly winds between 40 and 50 degrees south?
questions.explanation: With little land to slow them, westerlies in the far south blow hard, and clipper ships rode them for speed.

questions.question: What is it called when deep, cold, nutrient-rich water rises to the surface?
questions.explanation: Upwelling brings nutrients up to the sunlit layer, feeding plankton and some of the richest fishing grounds.

questions.question: What do sailors call the blue glow that can appear on masts during storms?
questions.explanation: St. Elmo's fire is a glowing electrical discharge from pointed objects when the air is highly charged, often in thunderstorms.

questions.question: What is an unusually large, unexpected wave on the open ocean called?
questions.explanation: A rogue wave is far taller than the waves around it. Once thought a sailors' tale, they have been measured by instruments.

questions.question: What is an underwater mountain that does not reach the surface called?
questions.explanation: Seamounts are usually extinct volcanoes, and they gather rich life as currents sweep around them.

questions.question: Which sea in the Atlantic is the only one with no land coastline?
questions.explanation: The Sargasso Sea is bounded by ocean currents, not land, and is known for its floating sargassum seaweed.

questions.question: Which passage separates the tip of South America from Antarctica?
questions.explanation: The Drake Passage is famous for some of the roughest seas on Earth.

questions.question: Which European sea is known for its low-salt, brackish water?
questions.explanation: Many rivers pour into the Baltic and its link to the open ocean is narrow, so its water is only lightly salty.

questions.question: What is the seasonal wind shift that brings heavy summer rain to South Asia?
questions.explanation: The monsoon reverses with the seasons. In summer, moist winds blow in from the Indian Ocean and drench the land.

questions.question: What is the cool counterpart of El Nino in the Pacific called?
questions.explanation: La Nina brings cooler than normal water to the eastern tropical Pacific, the opposite phase of El Nino.

questions.question: In the Northern Hemisphere, which way do hurricanes spin?
questions.explanation: The Coriolis effect turns northern storms counterclockwise. In the Southern Hemisphere they spin clockwise.

questions.question: Which scale rates hurricanes from Category 1 to Category 5?
questions.explanation: The Saffir-Simpson scale ranks hurricanes by their sustained wind speed.

questions.question: What is the rise in sea level pushed ashore by a storm's winds called?
questions.explanation: A storm surge can flood coasts far above normal high tide and is often the deadliest part of a hurricane.

questions.question: What does the Japanese word tsunami mean?
questions.explanation: Tsunami means harbor wave, from the Japanese words tsu, harbor, and nami, wave.

questions.question: Why does deep, clear seawater look blue?
questions.explanation: Water soaks up red and orange light more than blue, so blue light is what scatters back to our eyes.

questions.question: At about what temperature does ordinary seawater freeze?
questions.explanation: Salt lowers the freezing point, so seawater freezes at about 28°F, colder than fresh water.

questions.question: Going down in the sea, pressure rises by about one atmosphere every how far?
questions.explanation: Every 10 meters of seawater adds about one atmosphere of pressure on top of the air above.

questions.question: What do scientists call the drifting flakes of debris that sink to the deep sea?
questions.explanation: Marine snow is dead plankton, waste and dust drifting down, and it feeds much of the life in the deep.

questions.question: What do sailors call someone who has crossed the equator by sea?
questions.explanation: In the line crossing ceremony, first timers are pollywogs. Once they cross the equator they become shellbacks.

questions.question: What is the stretch of open water a wind blows over, shaping waves, called?
questions.explanation: The longer the fetch, along with wind speed and duration, the bigger the waves can grow.

questions.question: What is the net drift of surface water at right angles to the wind called?
questions.explanation: Because of Earth's spin, wind-driven water moves on average at 90 degrees to the wind, as Vagn Walfrid Ekman showed.

questions.question: What is a standing wave that sloshes back and forth in a bay or lake called?
questions.explanation: A seiche rocks a whole basin back and forth, like water in a tilted bathtub, often after wind or pressure changes.

questions.question: What is a wave that surges up a river on the incoming tide called?
questions.explanation: A tidal bore forms where a strong rising tide funnels into a narrowing river, pushing a wall of water upstream.

questions.question: What is a spot in the sea where the tidal range is close to zero called?
questions.explanation: Tides rotate around amphidromic points, and the range grows the farther you go from one.

questions.question: Which American founder published an early chart of the Gulf Stream?
questions.explanation: As deputy postmaster, Franklin worked with whaling captain Timothy Folger to chart the current, helping mail ships sail faster.

questions.question: What is a flat-topped underwater mountain called?
questions.explanation: A guyot is a seamount whose top was worn flat by waves when it stood at the surface, before it sank.

questions.question: Point Nemo, the spot in the sea farthest from any land, lies in which ocean?
questions.explanation: Point Nemo is in the South Pacific, more than 2,600 km from the nearest land.

questions.question: Which sea's deep water has almost no oxygen, preserving ancient shipwrecks?
questions.explanation: Below about 150 meters the Black Sea is nearly oxygen free, so wood eating creatures cannot destroy old wrecks.

questions.question: Compared with the Moon, how strong is the Sun's pull on the tides?
questions.explanation: The Sun is far bigger but much farther away, so its tide raising pull is a bit under half the Moon's.

questions.question: What is the icy tube of sinking brine that grows down from sea ice called?
questions.explanation: Very salty, very cold brine sinks from sea ice and freezes the water around it into a hollow icy finger.

questions.question: What is an area of open water surrounded by sea ice called?
questions.explanation: Polynyas are kept open by winds or upwelling warmer water, and they are key spots for seals and seabirds.

questions.question: After the Roaring Forties, what do sailors call the winds near 50 degrees south?
questions.explanation: The farther south, the wilder the winds: the Roaring Forties, the Furious Fifties, then the Screaming Sixties.

questions.question: The calm, high-pressure horse latitudes lie near which latitude?
questions.explanation: The horse latitudes sit near 30 degrees north and south, where sinking air brings light winds and dry weather.

questions.question: What is the steamy fog that forms when very cold air drifts over warmer sea?
questions.explanation: When frigid air moves over warmer water, the water evaporates and instantly condenses, rising like steam.

questions.question: In the deep open ocean, about how fast can a tsunami travel?
questions.explanation: In deep water a tsunami can move at 700 km/h or more. It slows and grows taller as it reaches shallow coasts.

questions.question: What is the average depth of the world's ocean?
questions.explanation: The ocean averages roughly 3,700 meters deep, about 12,100 feet.

questions.question: Measured from its base on the seafloor, which mountain is the tallest?
questions.explanation: Mauna Kea in Hawaii rises over 10,000 meters from the Pacific floor, though most of it is underwater.

questions.question: Which cape is the true southernmost point of Africa?
questions.explanation: Cape Agulhas, not the Cape of Good Hope, is Africa's southern tip and the official meeting point of the Atlantic and Indian oceans.

questions.question: The original Maelstrom whirlpool churns off the coast of which country?
questions.explanation: The Moskstraumen, the first Maelstrom, swirls among Norway's Lofoten Islands, driven by strong tidal currents.

questions.question: What is the giant ocean that surrounded the supercontinent Pangaea called?
questions.explanation: Panthalassa, Greek for all sea, covered most of the globe around Pangaea.

questions.question: Who led the first voyage to sail through the Northwest Passage?
questions.explanation: Amundsen took the small ship Gjoa through the Arctic passage north of Canada between 1903 and 1906.

questions.question: Which 1870s British voyage is credited with founding modern oceanography?
questions.explanation: HMS Challenger sailed from 1872 to 1876, sounding depths and collecting thousands of new species.

questions.question: In 1692, what disaster sank much of the pirate haven of Port Royal into the sea?
questions.explanation: On June 7, 1692 an earthquake struck Port Royal, Jamaica, and much of the town slid into the harbor.

questions.question: The old pirate haven of Port Royal sits on which Caribbean island?
questions.explanation: Port Royal lies at the tip of the Palisadoes spit guarding Kingston Harbour in Jamaica.

questions.question: Nassau, a famous pirate haven of the early 1700s, is now the capital of which nation?
questions.explanation: Nassau, once a lawless pirate port, is today the capital of the Bahamas.

questions.question: The buccaneer stronghold of Tortuga is an island off the coast of which modern country?
questions.explanation: Tortuga lies just off the north coast of Haiti, on the western side of Hispaniola.

questions.question: Spanish "pieces of eight" were coins made mostly of which metal?
questions.explanation: Pieces of eight were silver coins, minted largely from American silver and traded across the world.

questions.question: What was a doubloon?
questions.explanation: A doubloon was a Spanish gold coin worth two escudos, prized by pirates and merchants alike.

questions.question: What document let a privateer legally attack enemy ships?
questions.explanation: A letter of marque was a government license allowing a private ship to attack and seize enemy vessels.

questions.question: Which woman pirate sailed with Anne Bonny aboard Calico Jack's ship?
questions.explanation: Mary Read and Anne Bonny both sailed with Calico Jack Rackham until the crew's capture in 1720.

questions.question: According to early accounts, what did Blackbeard put under his hat to frighten his enemies?
questions.explanation: A 1724 history says Blackbeard tucked lit slow matches under his hat so smoke curled around his face in battle.

questions.question: Which sea was the busiest hunting ground for pirates of the Golden Age?
questions.explanation: The Caribbean, with its rich shipping lanes and hidden coves, was the heart of Golden Age piracy.

questions.question: Barbary corsairs sailed from ports along the coast of which region?
questions.explanation: The Barbary corsairs sailed from ports on the North African coast and raided shipping across the Mediterranean and beyond.

questions.question: What did it mean for a pirate to be "marooned"?
questions.explanation: Marooning meant abandoning someone on a remote island, often with little more than a pistol and some water.

questions.question: Francis Drake sailed as a privateer for which English monarch?
questions.explanation: Drake raided Spanish ships and ports in the service of Queen Elizabeth I, who knighted him in 1581.

questions.question: What was the name of the ship Francis Drake sailed around the world?
questions.explanation: Drake completed his voyage around the world in 1580 aboard the Golden Hind.

questions.question: What nickname was given to the pirate Bartholomew Roberts?
questions.explanation: Bartholomew Roberts is remembered as Black Bart, though the nickname seems to have caught on only after his death.

questions.question: Where did Calico Jack's nickname come from?
questions.explanation: John Rackham was called Calico Jack for the colorful calico cotton clothes he liked to wear.

questions.question: What nickname did the pirate Samuel Bellamy go by?
questions.explanation: Samuel Bellamy was known as Black Sam, reportedly for wearing his dark hair long and tied back.

questions.question: Which pirate port was nicknamed "the wickedest city on Earth"?
questions.explanation: Port Royal, Jamaica, was famous for its taverns, gambling and pirates, earning that grim nickname.

questions.question: In sailor slang, where is "Davy Jones' Locker"?
questions.explanation: Davy Jones' Locker is the bottom of the sea, the resting place of drowned sailors and sunken ships.

questions.question: Which punishment dragged a sailor under a ship's hull from one side to the other?
questions.explanation: Keelhauling pulled a sailor beneath the keel, where barnacles could cut badly. It was a naval punishment.

questions.question: What was the "cat o' nine tails" used for at sea?
questions.explanation: The cat o' nine tails was a whip with nine knotted cords used to flog sailors as punishment.

questions.question: On a sailing warship, what job did a "powder monkey" do?
questions.explanation: Powder monkeys were usually boys who ran gunpowder from the magazine up to the guns in battle.

questions.question: Grog, the classic sailor's drink, was rum mixed with what?
questions.explanation: Grog was rum watered down, often with lime or lemon added, to stretch the ration and keep crews steadier.

questions.question: An hourglass on a pirate flag warned victims of what?
questions.explanation: An hourglass told the crew of a target ship that their time was short and they should surrender quickly.

questions.question: How did most pirate crews choose their captain?
questions.explanation: Pirate captains were usually elected by the crew and could be voted out if the crew lost faith in them.

questions.question: What did sailors mean by "the Spanish Main"?
questions.explanation: The Spanish Main was the mainland coast of Spain's American empire around the Caribbean, rich in treasure ports.

questions.question: What name was given to the French and English raiders based on Hispaniola and Tortuga in the 1600s?
questions.explanation: The buccaneers began as hunters on Hispaniola and became raiders of Spanish shipping and towns.

questions.question: What small, fast, single-masted ship was a favorite of Caribbean pirates?
questions.explanation: Sloops were quick, nimble and shallow in draft, perfect for chasing prey and slipping into hidden coves.

questions.question: What were the big Spanish ships that carried American treasure home to Spain?
questions.explanation: Heavily armed galleons sailed in treasure fleets carrying silver and gold from the Americas to Spain.

questions.question: How did most pirate crews divide their plunder?
questions.explanation: Pirate articles set out shares for each crew member, with officers taking a little more than ordinary hands.

questions.question: Pirates often flew another nation's flag to sneak up on prey. What was this trick called?
questions.explanation: Flying false colors let pirates get close before raising their own flag and demanding surrender.

questions.question: In pirate talk, what does "booty" mean?
questions.explanation: Booty means plunder, the goods and treasure taken from a captured ship or town.

questions.question: Most Golden Age pirates had worked at what before turning to piracy?
questions.explanation: Most pirates were former merchant or navy sailors who already knew how to handle a ship.

questions.question: What did pirates hope would happen when they raised their flag at a target ship?
questions.explanation: Pirates wanted an easy prize. A frightening flag often made a crew give up without a fight.

questions.question: Besides coins, what did pirates most often take from captured ships?
questions.explanation: Most pirate plunder was ordinary cargo: food, rum, cloth, tools, medicine and spare sails and rope.

questions.question: A privateer's license allowed attacks on the ships of which nations?
questions.explanation: A privateer could only lawfully attack ships of nations at war with the government that licensed it.

questions.question: Which Royal Navy lieutenant led the attack that killed Blackbeard?
questions.explanation: Lieutenant Robert Maynard boarded Blackbeard's sloop at Ocracoke in November 1718, and Blackbeard died in the fight.

questions.question: After Blackbeard was killed, where did Lieutenant Maynard hang his head?
questions.explanation: Maynard hung Blackbeard's head from his sloop's bowsprit as proof the pirate was dead.

questions.question: Which governor arrived in Nassau in 1718 with a royal pardon to end its pirate days?
questions.explanation: Woodes Rogers arrived as royal governor of the Bahamas in 1718 and offered pirates the King's pardon.

questions.question: Castaway Alexander Selkirk's story is thought to have inspired which novel?
questions.explanation: Selkirk spent over four years alone on a Pacific island, and his tale is widely seen as a model for Robinson Crusoe.

questions.question: Stede Bonnet, a wealthy landowner who turned pirate, was nicknamed what?
questions.explanation: Bonnet was a rich, educated plantation owner with no sailing experience, earning him the name the Gentleman Pirate.

questions.question: On which Caribbean island did Stede Bonnet own a plantation before turning pirate?
questions.explanation: Stede Bonnet was a Barbados landowner who bought a sloop in 1717 and sailed off to become a pirate.

questions.question: Bartholomew Roberts came from which country?
questions.explanation: Bartholomew Roberts was born in Pembrokeshire, Wales, and served as a ship's mate before turning pirate.

questions.question: According to early accounts, what did Bartholomew Roberts drink instead of rum?
questions.explanation: The 1724 General History says Roberts was a sober captain who preferred tea to strong drink.

questions.question: How did Anne Bonny and Mary Read avoid being hanged right away in 1720?
questions.explanation: Both women "pleaded their bellies", and courts would not hang a pregnant woman, so their sentences were delayed.

questions.question: How did the career of pirate Henry Every end?
questions.explanation: After his huge 1695 prize, Henry Every disappeared with his loot and was never captured.

questions.question: After taking the royal pardon, Benjamin Hornigold became what?
questions.explanation: Hornigold accepted the King's pardon in 1718 and was sent out by Woodes Rogers to hunt his former comrades.

questions.question: Which future pirate legend learned the trade serving under Benjamin Hornigold?
questions.explanation: Edward Teach, later Blackbeard, served under Hornigold before taking his own command.

questions.question: Jean Lafitte and his crews helped American forces win which 1815 battle?
questions.explanation: Lafitte supplied fighters, flints and powder to Andrew Jackson for the Battle of New Orleans in January 1815.

questions.question: Irish pirate queen Grace O'Malley met which English monarch in 1593?
questions.explanation: Grace O'Malley sailed to England in 1593 and met Queen Elizabeth I face to face at Greenwich.

questions.question: What did the Spanish call Francis Drake?
questions.explanation: Spaniards called Drake El Draque, a play on his name that also suggested a dragon.

questions.question: In 1715, a hurricane wrecked a Spanish treasure fleet off which coast?
questions.explanation: The 1715 treasure fleet was wrecked off Florida's east coast, and salvagers and pirates rushed to the wrecks.

questions.question: A Spanish piece of eight was worth eight of which coin?
questions.explanation: The piece of eight was a silver peso of eight reales, which is where its name comes from.

questions.question: Which officer on a pirate ship shared out the loot and settled crew disputes?
questions.explanation: The quartermaster was elected by the crew and guarded their interests, from dividing plunder to keeping order.

questions.question: Which young Roman was kidnapped by pirates and later had them captured and executed?
questions.explanation: Ancient writers say the young Julius Caesar was held for ransom by pirates, then hunted them down once freed.

questions.question: What was "careening" a ship?
questions.explanation: Crews beached a ship and leaned it over to scrape weed and barnacles from the hull, which kept it fast.

questions.question: Treasure hunter Mel Fisher found which Spanish galleon off Florida in 1985?
questions.explanation: After a 16 year search, Mel Fisher's team found the Atocha, sunk in a 1622 hurricane, in the Florida Keys.

questions.question: Pieces of eight were often cut into parts. Which American slang for a quarter came from this?
questions.explanation: One eighth of a piece of eight was a bit, so a quarter dollar became known as two bits.

questions.question: When Blackbeard blockaded Charleston in 1718, what was his main ransom demand?
questions.explanation: Blackbeard held hostages and demanded a chest of medicine, which the town sent to win their release.

questions.question: The governor of which colony sent the expedition that killed Blackbeard?
questions.explanation: Virginia's governor Alexander Spotswood sent two sloops under Lieutenant Maynard to hunt Blackbeard down.

questions.question: Elizabeth I's privateers, such as Drake and Hawkins, were nicknamed what?
questions.explanation: The Sea Dogs raided Spanish treasure ships and colonies with the Queen's quiet blessing.

questions.question: The pirate port of Nassau stands on which island?
questions.explanation: Nassau sits on New Providence, a small Bahamian island whose shallow harbor sheltered pirate sloops.

questions.question: Which North African city was a major base for Barbary corsairs?
questions.explanation: Algiers, along with Tunis, Tripoli and Salé, sent out corsairs to raid Mediterranean and Atlantic shipping.

questions.question: What nationality was the cruel buccaneer François l'Olonnais?
questions.explanation: François l'Olonnais was a French buccaneer of the 1660s, notorious even among buccaneers for his cruelty.

questions.question: What went wrong at William Kidd's first hanging in 1701?
questions.explanation: The rope snapped at Kidd's first hanging, and he was hanged again moments later.

questions.question: What did the buccaneers of the Caribbean call their loose brotherhood?
questions.explanation: The Brethren of the Coast was the name for the buccaneer fellowship of Tortuga and Hispaniola.

questions.question: Which line in the US Marines' Hymn recalls the fight against Barbary pirates?
questions.explanation: "To the shores of Tripoli" honors Marines who fought in the First Barbary War of 1801 to 1805.

questions.question: Pirates hanged at London's Execution Dock were left until how many tides washed over them?
questions.explanation: By custom, bodies at Execution Dock were left on the shore until three tides had covered them.

questions.question: Whose 1709 expedition rescued castaway Alexander Selkirk from his island?
questions.explanation: Woodes Rogers, privateering in the Pacific, found Selkirk on Juan Fernández in 1709 after four years alone.

questions.question: Stede Bonnet bought his first pirate sloop instead of stealing it. What did he name it?
questions.explanation: Bonnet paid for and armed the sloop Revenge in 1717, unusual for a pirate.

questions.question: In which city was Stede Bonnet hanged in 1718?
questions.explanation: Bonnet was captured on the Cape Fear River, tried in Charleston and hanged there in December 1718.

questions.question: Bartholomew Roberts gave several of his flagships which name?
questions.explanation: Roberts named more than one of his flagships the Royal Fortune.

questions.question: What killed Bartholomew Roberts in his final battle in 1722?
questions.explanation: Roberts was struck in the throat by grapeshot, and his crew threw his body overboard as he had wished.

questions.question: What was the name of Henry Every's pirate ship?
questions.explanation: Every renamed the warship Charles II as the Fancy after he and the crew took her in a 1694 mutiny.

questions.question: Charles Vane, who refused the King's pardon, was hanged in 1721 at which port?
questions.explanation: Vane was captured after a shipwreck, tried in Jamaica and hanged at Gallows Point, Port Royal.

questions.question: Jean Lafitte's smuggling base near New Orleans lay in which body of water?
questions.explanation: Lafitte's Baratarians operated from Grande Terre island in Barataria Bay, south of New Orleans.

questions.question: Before being renamed, Francis Drake's Golden Hind was called what?
questions.explanation: Drake renamed the Pelican the Golden Hind in 1578, honoring his patron Christopher Hatton's crest.

questions.question: Spain's Manila galleons crossed the Pacific between Manila and which Mexican port?
questions.explanation: For 250 years Manila galleons linked the Philippines and Acapulco, carrying silver west and silks and spices east.

questions.question: Under Bartholomew Roberts' articles, how many pieces of eight did a sailor get for losing a limb?
questions.explanation: Roberts' articles promised 800 dollars from the common stock to any sailor who lost a limb or was crippled.

questions.question: Under Bartholomew Roberts' articles, at what hour did lights and candles go out?
questions.explanation: Roberts' articles ordered lights out at eight at night, and anyone drinking later had to do it on open deck.

questions.question: In pirate articles, "Moses's Law" was a whipping of how many lashes?
questions.explanation: Moses's Law meant 40 lashes save one, so 39 strokes on the bare back, as in John Phillips' articles.

questions.question: Calico Jack's body was hung in a gibbet on an islet near Port Royal now named for him. What is it?
questions.explanation: Rackham's body was displayed on a tiny cay at the entrance to Port Royal, and it still bears his name.

questions.question: Before Blackbeard took her, the Queen Anne's Revenge was a French ship named what?
questions.explanation: Blackbeard captured the French slave ship La Concorde in 1717 and refitted her as Queen Anne's Revenge.

questions.question: What object found in 1985 proved a wreck off Cape Cod was Black Sam Bellamy's Whydah?
questions.explanation: Divers raised a bell inscribed THE WHYDAH GALLY 1716, the first pirate wreck ever positively identified.

questions.question: In 1668, Henry Morgan captured which fortified Spanish port on the Panama coast?
questions.explanation: Morgan's buccaneers seized Portobelo in 1668 and held it for ransom before sailing back to Jamaica.

questions.question: What did William Kidd use to kill his gunner William Moore in 1697?
questions.explanation: In a quarrel, Kidd struck gunner William Moore with an iron-bound bucket. Moore died the next day.

questions.question: Which buccaneer and explorer was the first person to sail around the world three times?
questions.explanation: William Dampier, a buccaneer turned writer and navigator, completed three circumnavigations by 1711.

questions.question: Which Welsh pirate captain forced Bartholomew Roberts into piracy in 1719?
questions.explanation: Howell Davis captured Roberts' ship off West Africa. When Davis was killed weeks later, the crew elected Roberts.

questions.question: Much of Spain's silver came from a great mine at Potosí. Which country is it in today?
questions.explanation: The Cerro Rico of Potosí, now in Bolivia, produced vast silver that became Spanish coins like pieces of eight.

questions.question: Bartholomew Roberts' flag showed him standing on two skulls. Which islands' people did they mock?
questions.explanation: The skulls were marked ABH and AMH, a Barbadian's head and a Martinican's head, for governors who hunted him.

questions.question: What name was given to the pirates who raided the coasts of China and Korea from the 1200s to the 1500s?
questions.explanation: The wokou, at first largely Japanese and later mixed crews, raided East Asian coasts for centuries.

questions.question: Fish and chips is a classic takeaway dish from which country?
questions.explanation: Fried battered fish with chips became a working-class staple in England in the 1800s and is still sold in chip shops nationwide.

questions.question: Thin slices of raw fish served without rice are called what in Japanese cuisine?
questions.explanation: Sashimi is sliced raw fish or seafood served on its own, often with soy sauce and wasabi. Sushi always involves vinegared rice.

questions.question: Gravlax, a Scandinavian dish cured with salt, sugar and dill, is made from which fish?
questions.explanation: Gravlax is raw salmon cured in salt, sugar and dill. The name comes from an old practice of burying the fish to cure it.

questions.question: True caviar is the salted roe of which kind of fish?
questions.explanation: Caviar traditionally means salt-cured sturgeon eggs. Eggs from other fish are sold as roe, such as salmon roe.

questions.question: What are a fish's eggs called when they are eaten as food?
questions.explanation: Roe is the egg mass of a fish. Milt is the male's sperm, and fry are newly hatched young fish.

questions.question: What tool do ice anglers use to drill a hole through a frozen lake?
questions.explanation: An ice auger is a large spiral drill, turned by hand or motor, that bores a round hole through the ice.

questions.question: A small hut set up on a frozen lake to shelter ice anglers is commonly called what?
questions.explanation: Ice shanties, also called fish houses, keep anglers out of the wind while they fish through holes in the floor.

questions.question: Which bait worm is named for coming up to the surface after dark?
questions.explanation: Nightcrawlers are large earthworms that come out on damp nights, which is when anglers often gather them.

questions.question: Artificial flies used in fly fishing most often imitate what?
questions.explanation: Most flies imitate insects such as mayflies, caddisflies and stoneflies, though some copy small fish or crustaceans.

questions.question: Manhattan clam chowder has what kind of base, unlike creamy New England chowder?
questions.explanation: Manhattan clam chowder uses a red, tomato-based broth, while New England chowder is made with milk or cream.

questions.question: Paella, often cooked with shrimp, mussels and clams, comes from which country?
questions.explanation: Paella comes from Valencia in eastern Spain. It is cooked in a wide shallow pan, and seafood versions are popular along the coast.

questions.question: Ceviche, a Latin American dish of raw fish, is cured in what?
questions.explanation: In ceviche, lime or lemon juice firms up the raw fish and turns it opaque without heat.

questions.question: Fishing line made from a single strand of nylon is called what?
questions.explanation: Mono is short for monofilament: one solid strand of nylon. Braided line is woven from many thin fibers.

questions.question: What is the backward-facing point on a fishhook that keeps a fish from slipping off?
questions.explanation: The barb sits just behind the point. Barbless hooks are easier to remove, which helps when releasing fish.

questions.question: Which net is thrown by hand so it spreads into a circle before sinking?
questions.explanation: A cast net has weights around its edge. Thrown well, it opens into a circle and sinks over a school of baitfish.

questions.question: What do anglers use to scoop a hooked fish out of the water?
questions.explanation: A landing net has a handle and a deep bag, so a tired fish can be lifted from the water without breaking the line.

questions.question: Lobsters are commonly caught in what kind of baited cage?
questions.explanation: Lobster pots, or traps, let a lobster crawl in after bait but make it hard to crawl back out.

questions.question: In angling, what does it mean to set the hook?
questions.explanation: Setting the hook is a quick, firm pull on the rod after a bite, driving the hook point into the fish's mouth.

questions.question: What do anglers call a curved metal lure shaped like the bowl of a kitchen utensil?
questions.explanation: Spoon lures are curved metal blades that wobble and flash as they move through the water, like a small baitfish.

questions.question: Which Japanese dish features seafood and vegetables in a light, crisp batter?
questions.explanation: Tempura is seafood and vegetables dipped in a light batter and deep fried. Shrimp tempura is a classic.

questions.question: Fugu, served in Japan only by specially licensed chefs, is which fish?
questions.explanation: Fugu is pufferfish. Parts of it contain a deadly toxin, so chefs must train and be licensed to prepare it.

questions.question: British fish and chips is traditionally served with a side of mushy what?
questions.explanation: Mushy peas are dried marrowfat peas soaked and simmered into a thick green mash, a chip shop favorite.

questions.question: Poke, a salad of cubed raw fish, comes from which U.S. state?
questions.explanation: Poke comes from Hawaii. The word means to slice or cut crosswise, and ahi tuna is a common choice.

questions.question: Gumbo, a stew often full of shrimp and crab, is most associated with which state?
questions.explanation: Gumbo is a signature dish of Louisiana, blending French, West African and Native influences in a thick, rich stew.

questions.question: What reel setting lets line slip under tension so a strong fish cannot snap it?
questions.explanation: The drag is an adjustable brake. When a fish pulls harder than the set tension, line slips off instead of breaking.

questions.question: What are the rings along a fishing rod that the line passes through?
questions.explanation: Guides spread the strain of a fish along the rod and keep the line running smoothly from reel to tip.

questions.question: In 'The Old Man and the Sea', what giant fish does Santiago battle?
questions.explanation: Hemingway's old fisherman hooks a huge marlin and fights it for days, only to have sharks eat it on the way home.

questions.question: In fly fishing, what does 'matching the hatch' mean?
questions.explanation: Matching the hatch means choosing a fly that looks like the insects hatching on the water at that moment.

questions.question: What is bycatch?
questions.explanation: Bycatch is anything netted or hooked that the fishers were not targeting, such as turtles, dolphins or young fish.

questions.question: Noodling is the sport of catching which fish with bare hands?
questions.explanation: Noodlers reach into underwater holes and let a big catfish bite their hand, then haul it out. It is popular in the southern U.S.

questions.question: Which billfish is named for its tall, flag-like dorsal fin?
questions.explanation: The sailfish can raise a huge dorsal fin like a sail. It folds the fin down into a groove when swimming fast.

questions.question: What small rotating connector stops a spinning lure from twisting the line?
questions.explanation: A swivel has two rings joined by a spinning barrel, so a twisting lure does not twist the whole line.

questions.question: How many points does a treble hook have?
questions.explanation: A treble hook is three hooks joined at the shank, giving three points. They are common on plugs and crankbaits.

questions.question: An old rule says to eat oysters only in months that contain which letter?
questions.explanation: The R-month rule skips May through August, when warm water once made oysters riskier and they are busy spawning.

questions.question: Anglers use a fish finder to spot fish using what?
questions.explanation: A fish finder sends sound pulses down and reads the echoes, showing the bottom, fish and bait schools on a screen.

questions.question: Polarized sunglasses help anglers by cutting what?
questions.explanation: Polarized lenses block reflected light off the surface, letting anglers see into the water and spot fish.

questions.question: Why do fishing rules often set a minimum mesh size for nets?
questions.explanation: Larger mesh lets small, young fish swim through, so they can grow up and breed before they are caught.

questions.question: What slang word do anglers use for an unusually big fish?
questions.explanation: A lunker is a big, heavy fish. Minnows, fingerlings and tiddlers are all words for small ones.

questions.question: What do anglers call the wicker basket used to carry their catch?
questions.explanation: A creel is a woven basket, traditionally wicker, worn on a strap. Daily catch limits are still often called creel limits.

questions.question: Bacalao, popular in Spain and Portugal, is which fish salted and dried?
questions.explanation: Salt cod, bacalao in Spain and bacalhau in Portugal, was dried hard to keep for months and soaked before cooking.

questions.question: Surströmming, a famously pungent Swedish delicacy, is fermented what?
questions.explanation: Surströmming is Baltic herring fermented in barrels and then in cans, which often bulge from the gases inside.

questions.question: Fish sauce, used in Thai and Vietnamese cooking, is usually made from fermented what?
questions.explanation: Fish sauce is made by layering anchovies with salt and letting them ferment for months, then draining off the liquid.

questions.question: On a sushi menu, what is unagi?
questions.explanation: Unagi is freshwater eel, usually grilled with a sweet glaze. Saltwater eel is called anago.

questions.question: What do Japanese chefs call the fatty belly meat of bluefin tuna?
questions.explanation: Toro is the rich, fatty belly of tuna. Ebi is shrimp, saba is mackerel and tako is octopus.

questions.question: At a traditional New England clambake, what is layered over the food to steam it?
questions.explanation: Clambakes cook clams, lobster and corn over hot rocks under a thick blanket of wet seaweed, which makes the steam.

questions.question: Bouillabaisse, a famous fish stew, comes from which French port city?
questions.explanation: Bouillabaisse began as a fishers' stew in Marseille, made from the bony rockfish they could not sell.

questions.question: Which reel has a fixed spool and a wire bail that flips open for casting?
questions.explanation: On a spinning reel the spool does not turn as you cast. Opening the bail lets line spiral off the end.

questions.question: On a baitcasting reel, what is a tangled overrun of line called?
questions.explanation: A backlash happens when the spool spins faster than line leaves it, leaving a snarl anglers call a bird's nest.

questions.question: A reel with a 6.2:1 gear ratio turns its spool how often per handle turn?
questions.explanation: Gear ratio is spool turns per crank. Higher ratios pick up line faster, while lower ones give more cranking power.

questions.question: What do fly anglers call the extra line wound onto the reel beneath the fly line?
questions.explanation: Backing fills the spool and gives extra length when a strong fish runs past the end of the fly line.

questions.question: Which fishing line is hard to see underwater because it bends light much like water?
questions.explanation: Fluorocarbon has a refractive index close to water, so it nearly disappears. It also sinks faster than nylon.

questions.question: Compared with monofilament, braided line is known for having almost no what?
questions.explanation: Braid barely stretches, so every bite is felt clearly and hooksets are strong. Mono stretches noticeably.

questions.question: A fast action fishing rod bends mostly where?
questions.explanation: Rod action says where a rod flexes. Fast rods bend near the tip, while slow rods bend down toward the handle.

questions.question: Classic split-cane fly rods are made from strips of what?
questions.explanation: Split-cane rods are built from tapered bamboo strips glued together, usually into a six-sided blank.

questions.question: In fly fishing, a 5-weight rod is matched to what?
questions.explanation: Fly rods are rated by the weight of line they cast best. A 5-weight rod is built to cast a 5-weight line.

questions.question: What is the thin final section of a fly leader that the fly is tied to?
questions.explanation: The tippet is the finest piece at the end of the leader. Anglers replace it as it gets shorter from changing flies.

questions.question: In fly fishing, a nymph imitates which stage of an insect's life?
questions.explanation: Nymphs copy young aquatic insects living on the stream bed, which is where trout do much of their feeding.

questions.question: Which fly cast works with no room behind the angler by rolling line along the water?
questions.explanation: The roll cast needs no back cast. The angler sweeps the rod forward and a loop rolls out across the water.

questions.question: Which 1653 book by Izaak Walton celebrates the joys of fishing?
questions.explanation: Izaak Walton's The Compleat Angler mixes fishing advice with country life and is one of the most reprinted books in English.

questions.question: Norman Maclean's novella about fly fishing brothers in Montana is called what?
questions.explanation: A River Runs Through It, published in 1976, follows two brothers and their minister father on Montana's rivers.

questions.question: Which strong hook knot is tied by passing a doubled line through the hook eye?
questions.explanation: The Palomar is tied with a doubled line pushed through the eye, an overhand knot, then the hook passed through the loop.

questions.question: Which knot joins two lines of similar thickness with wraps on each side?
questions.explanation: The blood knot, also called a barrel knot, twists the two line ends around each other and tucks them through the middle.

questions.question: A seine net hangs straight down in the water with what along its top edge?
questions.explanation: A seine has floats on the top line and weights on the bottom line, so it stands like a wall to encircle fish.

questions.question: The ama divers of Japan traditionally free dive to gather what?
questions.explanation: Ama divers, mostly women, dive on one breath for abalone, other shellfish and seaweed, a tradition many centuries old.

questions.question: Fishers on Sri Lanka's south coast are famous for fishing while perched on what?
questions.explanation: Stilt fishers sit on a crossbar tied to a pole set in the surf and catch small fish with a rod and line.

questions.question: Kochi, in India, is famous for giant shore-operated nets known as what?
questions.explanation: Kochi's huge cantilevered nets are lowered into the water and raised with counterweights. They are called Chinese fishing nets.

questions.question: Tenkara, a style of fly fishing that uses no reel, comes from which country?
questions.explanation: Tenkara is a Japanese mountain stream method using a long rod with line tied straight to the tip, with no reel at all.

questions.question: What do the tall outriggers on a sportfishing boat do?
questions.explanation: Outriggers are long poles that hold lines far out to the sides, so several baits can be trolled without tangling.

questions.question: Circle hooks are favored for catch and release because they usually hook a fish where?
questions.explanation: A circle hook slides out of the throat and turns into the jaw corner, which makes swallowed hooks much less common.

questions.question: In standard fishhook sizing, which of these is the largest hook?
questions.explanation: For ordinary hook sizes, a bigger number means a smaller hook. Sizes with a slash, like 2/0, grow larger instead.

questions.question: Sushi with a slice of fish pressed onto a hand-formed mound of rice is called what?
questions.explanation: Nigiri means hand-pressed. Maki is rolled in seaweed, temaki is a cone and chirashi is fish scattered over a bowl of rice.

questions.question: Hákarl, Iceland's famous fermented delicacy, is made from what?
questions.explanation: Hákarl is Greenland shark meat, fermented and hung to dry for months to make it safe to eat. Its smell is famous.

questions.question: Moqueca, a seafood stew cooked with coconut milk, comes from which country?
questions.explanation: Moqueca is a Brazilian fish stew, especially from Bahia, made with coconut milk, palm oil, tomatoes and peppers.

questions.question: Cioppino, a tomato and seafood stew, was created by Italian fishers in which U.S. city?
questions.explanation: Cioppino was born on San Francisco's wharves, where Italian fishing families cooked the day's mixed catch in a tomato broth.

questions.question: Fisheries biologists often survey streams by briefly stunning fish with what?
questions.explanation: Electrofishing passes a current through the water that stuns fish for a moment so they can be counted and released.

questions.question: Which knot is used to tie backing onto the spool of a fly reel?
questions.explanation: The arbor knot cinches line around the center of the spool, called the arbor. It is the first knot on a new reel.

questions.question: What does a Bimini twist create?
questions.explanation: The Bimini twist twists a long loop of line on itself, making a doubled section that keeps nearly full line strength.

questions.question: The uni knot is also widely known by what other name?
questions.explanation: The uni knot was popularized by Vic Dunaway, but it is the same knot as the Duncan loop credited to Norman Duncan.

questions.question: Which knot joins a thin line to a much thicker line or wire?
questions.explanation: The Albright knot folds the thick line into a loop and wraps the thin line around it, ideal for unequal diameters.

questions.question: Which knot, first tied around a small nail or tube, joins fly line to a leader?
questions.explanation: The nail knot gets its name from the nail once used as a guide while wrapping the leader around the fly line.

questions.question: What is the joint where the sections of a two-piece rod fit together called?
questions.explanation: A ferrule is the fitted joint between rod sections. Old rods used metal sleeves, while modern ones often slide blank into blank.

questions.question: What is the bare shaft of a fishing rod called, before the guides and handle are added?
questions.explanation: Rod builders start with a blank, a hollow tube of graphite, fiberglass or bamboo, and then add the handle, seat and guides.

questions.question: Which fly cast uses a pull of the line hand on each stroke to add line speed?
questions.explanation: In the double haul the free hand tugs the line on both the back cast and forward cast, letting the line shoot much farther.

questions.question: In pole-and-line tuna fishing, crews spray what onto the surface to mimic a feeding frenzy?
questions.explanation: Sprinklers splash water onto the sea so it looks like baitfish are boiling at the surface, which keeps tuna biting.

questions.question: In which decade did a United Nations moratorium halt large-scale high seas driftnets?
questions.explanation: A 1991 UN resolution called for a global moratorium on large-scale high seas driftnet fishing from the end of 1992.

questions.question: A leister, used by Arctic and Scandinavian fishers, is what kind of tool?
questions.explanation: A leister is a spear with a central point and side prongs that grip the fish, used through ice or in shallow rivers.

questions.question: A coracle, a small round boat used for river fishing, is most associated with which country?
